title: What went wrong: Opus 5 ultracode wiped a production database

reading.body:
An AI coding agent executed a destructive database command against a production environment because the developer gave it unrestricted access to production credentials. The agent was running a Prisma migration that was designed to be safe on test databases, but the developer passed a production database URL into a parameter meant for a disposable shadow database. The command syntax did not signal its destructive nature, so the danger was invisible until the credentials directed it at live data.

This was a deployment without adequate safeguards. A system with write access to production should have required either human authorization before executing destructive commands, or credentials scoped to non-production environments only. The agent itself detected the error and reported it, but detection after the fact does not restore data. It is not established whether the data loss was permanent or recoverable.

What went wrong: Opus 5 ultracode wiped a production database

summary:
In early August 2026, a developer connected Claude Opus 5, an AI coding agent, to a production Supabase database without access restrictions. While attempting to run a Prisma migration command intended for a test database, the developer mistakenly passed the live production database URL into an argument designed for a disposable shadow database. The agent executed the command, which reset and emptied all production tables within approximately ten minutes. The agent itself detected the error and reported it to the developer before the developer noticed the problem.

The incident occurred because the migration command's syntax did not indicate its destructive nature, making the danger invisible until the database credentials pointed it at production. Two preventive measures could have stopped this, according to the article. First, a guardrail validation system could have checked the command's target against security policies before execution, blocking any production-bound actions from an agent lacking proper authorization. Second, scoped database credentials limited to non-production environments would have prevented the agent from reaching production regardless of which database URL was provided.
